items.name: Psychology -- CONTROL r0
items.response:
Adjudication between these two readings proceeds by turning the fidelity of the replicating study and the evidential base of the original literature into objects of measurement rather than matters of assertion, and the ego depletion controversy shows how that procedure works in practice. Because Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Muraven and Tice published the original ego depletion experiments in 1998, Hagger and colleagues subsequently coordinated a multi-laboratory registered replication of ego depletion across 23 laboratories. Either the 2016 Registered Replication Report found no statistically significant ego depletion effect, or it found a statistically significant effect; exactly one of these outcomes is the case, and the standing of the paradigm turns on which.

The first line of defence for a contested original finding is always the competence of the replication. Baumeister argued that the letter-crossing manipulation used in the replication was too weak to induce depletion. That objection cannot be squared with the design actually implemented, since the registered replication of ego depletion used the Stroop task as its depletion manipulation; the two descriptions of the procedure cannot both be correct. Whereas such an appeal to procedural weakness is raised once the outcome is known, Registered Replication Reports require the original authors to review the replication protocol before data collection begins, which is precisely what makes after-the-fact complaints about the protocol so difficult to sustain.

The second line of attack runs in the opposite direction, interrogating the original record rather than the new one. The null outcome of the multi-laboratory project indicates that the published estimate of the ego depletion effect in the original literature was inflated. At least one of two accounts of the discrepancy must hold, and perhaps both do: the inflation of that published estimate, or a failure of the task used in the multi-laboratory replication to induce a state of depletion in participants. Even though the task used in the multi-laboratory replication failed to induce a state of depletion in participants, Carter and McCullough reported small-study effects indicative of publication bias in the ego depletion literature, so the original record cannot be taken at face value either. The bias-corrected meta-analytic estimate of ego depletion reported by Carter and McCullough was d = 0.62.

The social priming disputes were adjudicated by a different instrument, namely the deliberate manipulation of the suspected artefact itself. Bargh, Chen and Burrows reported in 1996 that priming elderly stereotypes slowed participants' walking speed, and that report prompted Doyen and colleagues to report in 2012 that walking speed slowed only when the experimenters expected slowing. Because expectancy was varied experimentally rather than merely invoked, the replication failure carried information about mechanism and not just about effect size, and this is the feature that distinguishes a diagnostic replication from an inconclusive one. As a direct result of that expectancy finding, Daniel Kahneman circulated an open letter in 2012 urging social priming researchers to organise chains of replications. The Doyen result is what brought the letter about; without it Kahneman would not have written.

What emerges from both episodes is a set of criteria rather than a verdict delivered case by case: pre-registration of protocols with the original authors' assent, multi-site designs that make laboratory-specific competence testable, bias-corrected synthesis of the original literature, and experimental manipulation of the artefacts that defenders of an effect propose. Where these conditions are met, the hypothesis that the replicating study was flawed becomes a testable claim with consequences, and the two possibilities can be separated empirically rather than by appeals to the tacit skill of the original investigators.
